chunks: Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id from Fadala from Hammad ibn 'Uthman from Isḥāq ibn 'Ammār from al-Mu'alla ibn Khunays, who said:

I heard Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) giving the Adhan, so he said: 'Allahu Akbar, Allahu Akbar, Allahu Akbar, Allahu Akbar. Ashhadu an la ilaha illa Allah, Ashhadu an la ilaha illa Allah. Ashhadu anna Muhammadan Rasul Allah, Ashhadu anna Muhammadan Rasul Allah. Hayya 'ala al-salat, Hayya 'ala al-salat. Hayya 'ala al-falah, Hayya 'ala al-falah.' Until he finished the Adhan, and he said at the end: 'Allahu Akbar, Allahu Akbar. La ilaha illa Allah, La ilaha illa Allah.'

As for the first two hadiths, although they included the mention of 'Allahu Akbar' twice at the beginning of the Adhan, it is permissible that he restricted himself to that because he intended to convey to the questioner the manner of pronouncing it, and it was known to him that restricting oneself to it without the four times is not sufficient. And that which reveals what we mentioned, that it is not permissible to restrict oneself to twice with choice, is what he narrated:
ai.seo_question: How many times should 'Allahu Akbar' be repeated at the beginning of the Adhan according to Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: This narration from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* details the precise recitation of the Adhan by Imam al-Sadiq (AS), emphasizing the fourfold repetition of 'Allahu Akbar' as the standard ritual form. The accompanying commentary clarifies that narrations citing only two repetitions serve an instructional purpose to demonstrate the phrasing, rather than indicating a valid minimal limit, thereby reinforcing the Shia jurisprudential view of the Adhan's complete structure. This distinction highlights the scholarly method of reconciling apparent textual variations through the lens of practical ritual validity.
